title: Surge, in real time
arc: Tomas wants surge pricing that reacts within a minute, not the next morning. That means streaming: Kafka, delivery guarantees, Structured Streaming, schemas that change, and failure handling. Midweek a single poison message stalls a partition and lag climbs past a million. By Friday demand per zone updates every minute, a bad record waits in a dead-letter queue instead of stopping the stream, and you have argued for one shared Kafka instead of one per team.
previously: Why is "exactly once" harder in a stream than in a batch?
Recall: what does a Kafka consumer commit, the last offset read or the next one?
What does a watermark decide about a late event?
Why does adding consumers past the partition count do nothing?
cliff: A concert ends at 10:30. When should prices move, and from which data?
One bad event stopped a partition. What keeps the rest of the stream moving?
After a restart, one record is processed twice. Which number was committed?
The warehouse and the trips database disagree by 312 rows. Which one is the truth?

scenes.monday: Tomas: "When a concert ends, prices should move in a minute, not tomorrow." You sketch a stream. Start with why streaming is harder than batch.
scenes.midweek: Lag passes 1.8 million. One malformed event, after an app release, stops a partition cold. Send it to a dead-letter queue and fix the offset that replays a record after a restart.
scenes.friday: Partitions cap parallelism: prove it in the simulator. Then three teams each want their own Kafka "so nobody breaks it". Decide, and bring them along.
